title: Finetuning discriminator left for future work
description: The authors note that further improvements could be made by finetuning the discriminator's representations, but they leave this for future work.

verdict.reasoning: Paper 2 directly solves the gap: it presents a multi-stage GAN pipeline where discriminators are systematically fine-tuned for a downstream task (generating topological insulators). The discriminator is replaced with one fine-tuned on a small target dataset, and a universal force field (CHGNet) is deployed as a fine-tuned discriminator to bias generation toward dynamically stable and insulating materials. This yields a >400% improvement in success rate. The gap—whether and how to fine-tune a discriminator's representations for downstream tasks—is squarely addressed with concrete results. Paper 1 is not relevant (it uses joint training from scratch with adaptive loss weights, not fine-tuning pre-trained discriminator representations).

paper.title: GANDALF: Generative Adversarial Networks with Discriminator-Adaptive Loss Fine-tuning for Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis from MRI
paper.abstract: Positron Emission Tomography (PET) is now regarded as the gold standard for the diagnosis of Alzheimer's Disease (AD). However, PET imaging can be prohibitive in terms of cost and planning, and is also among the imaging techniques with the highest dosage of radiation. Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI), in contrast, is more widely available and provides more flexibility when setting the desired image resolution. Unfortunately, the diagnosis of AD using MRI is difficult due to the very subtle physiological differences between healthy and AD subjects visible on MRI. As a result, many attempts have been made to synthesize PET images from MR images using generative adversarial networks (GANs) in the interest of enabling the diagnosis of AD from MR. Existing work on PET synthesis from MRI has largely focused on Conditional GANs, where MR images are used to generate PET images and subsequently used for AD diagnosis. There is no end-to-end training goal. This paper proposes an alternative approach to the aforementioned, where AD diagnosis is incorporated in the GAN training objective to achieve the best AD classification performance. Different GAN lossesare fine-tuned based on the discriminator performance, and the overall training is stabilized. The proposed network architecture and training regime show state-of-the-art performance for three- and four- class AD classification tasks.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper proposes GANDALF, a GAN that synthesizes PET from MRI while jointly training for AD classification. The discriminator is trained from scratch with both a GAN loss and an AD classification loss, with adaptive weighting of these losses during training. The "fine-tuning" in the paper refers to adaptively adjusting loss weights (hyperparameters λ) during training, not to finetuning a pre-trained discriminator's representations for downstream tasks.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap specifically concerns finetuning the discriminator's representations (i.e., taking a pre-trained discriminator and adapting its learned features for downstream tasks). This paper does not explore that direction at all. The discriminator is trained from scratch jointly with the generator, and the "fine-tuning" described is about dynamically adjusting loss weights during training, not about finetuning pre-trained representations. The question of whether and how to finetune a discriminator's learned representations for downstream classification tasks remains entirely unexplored.
evidence_snippets: The $D$ in our generative network is trained with additional AD classification losses: (1) based on real MRI and generated PET input, multiplied by a hyper-parameter $\lambda_{GAN_D}$, and (2) based on real MRI and PET, multiplied by $\lambda_{CLS_D}$

In the earlier phase of the GAN training, generated PET likely are far from the real ones. They progressively become more realistic as the training proceeds. Therefore, $D$ is trained initially with small $\lambda_{GAN_D}$ and gradually increased during the training, while $\lambda_{CLS_D}$ starts from a larger value and gradually decreased.

Finding a better/deeper classifier/discriminator architecture could improve the final classification performance. However this should be balanced with the generator architecture/depth for the GAN training with the minimax objective.

paper.title: Fine tuning generative adversarial networks with universal force fields: application to two-dimensional topological insulators
paper.abstract: Despite rapid growth in use cases for generative artificial intelligence, its ability to design purpose built crystalline materials remains in a nascent phase. At the moment inverse design is generally accomplished by either constraining the training data set or producing a vast number of samples from a generator network and constraining the output via post-processing. We show that a general adversarial network trained to produce crystal structures from a latent space can be fine tuned through the introduction of advanced graph neural networks as discriminators, including a universal force field, to intrinsically bias the network towards generation of target materials. This is exemplified utilizing two-dimensional topological insulators as a sample target space. While a number of two-dimensional topological insulators have been predicted, the size of the band-gap, a measure of topological protection, remains a concern in most candidate compounds. The resulting generative network is shown to yield novel topological insulators.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper directly addresses the gap of finetuning discriminator representations for downstream tasks. It presents a multi-stage GAN training pipeline where discriminators are systematically fine-tuned: (1) a baseline GAN is trained on the C2DB database, (2) the discriminator is replaced with one fine-tuned on a small dataset of 962 topological materials to bias toward topological phases, and (3) a universal force field (CHGNet) is fine-tuned and used as a discriminator alongside a crystal graph convolutional network to bias toward dynamically stable and insulating materials. The paper demonstrates that this fine-tuning approach increases the success rate of generating target materials (topological insulators) by over 400% compared to baseline methods.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper fully solves the gap: it demonstrates that finetuning discriminator representations (including using a universal force field as a discriminator) is feasible and effective for downstream materials design tasks. No part of the gap remains unaddressed.
evidence_snippets: We show that a general adversarial network trained to produce crystal structures from a latent space can be fine tuned through the introduction of advanced graph neural networks as discriminators, including a universal force field, to intrinsically bias the network towards generation of target materials.

The first stage of fine-tuning considers a smaller dataset of 962 two-dimensional topological materials, the discriminator introduced in this stage distinguishes real samples supporting non-trivial topology...

The second fine-tuning stage leverages the power of MLiPs, specifically CHGNet. A custom discriminator layer calls this MLiP, relaxing the generated structure and computing the phonon density of states.
